name: Economies of Scale

claims.claim_text: At production volumes the engineering effort justified by a unit cost saving is large: a hundred thousand boards will support a hundred thousand dollars of labour to remove a dollar from each one.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're producing a hundred thousand boards, you can afford to spend a hundred thousand dollars in labor to actually get your cost down by a dollar
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cores, Digikey, Electronic Design - The Commercial Competitor Commencement

claims.claim_text: That arithmetic drives substitutions that would look absurd at small scale, such as fitting two of a cheaper resistance value in parallel to synthesise a more expensive one, saving a cent that becomes ten thousand dollars across a million units.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you put two 10, 10 Ks in parallel, you have a 5K resistor, but now you just saved a cent
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: Bill of materials optimisation also works by eliminating part numbers rather than by unit price: wiring one of an already-stocked transistor type as a diode avoids buying a whole reel of diodes for a single position.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually better to, um, wire one of those transistors as a diode
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: The deeper reason is that each distinct part consumes a feeder position on the assembly machine, so a design with thirty part numbers requires a machine that can hold thirty reels to be built efficiently.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need a machine that has 30 different reels on the SMD line to manufacture it efficiently
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: The price reductions available in the volume ranges most small producers occupy are modest: moving from a hundred units to a thousand yields something like ten percent rather than a halving.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't save much over a hundred
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Jersey Jeff Jactitation

claims.claim_text: The dramatic reductions associated with volume manufacturing require tens of thousands or a hundred thousand units, which is far beyond where most projects sit.
claims.quote_verbatim: The volumes have to be, I'm talking, you know, tens of thousands, maybe even a hundred thousand
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Jersey Jeff Jactitation

claims.claim_text: There is no threshold at which cost suddenly falls by an order of magnitude, so moving from ten thousand to a hundred thousand units does not transform the base cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's almost no magical limit where it suddenly becomes, you know, an order of magnitude cheaper
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: A representative assembly quotation shows the shape of the curve: roughly fifty-two dollars for a single board, forty-five at ten, about thirty-five at a hundred and about twenty-three at a thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's $52 for one board. Then if I type in 10 boards, it drops down to $45.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: The common expectation that a fifty-dollar single board implies a five-dollar board at a thousand units is simply wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: People might think, oh, if it's $50 for one board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Cost against volume is a step function with discontinuities rather than a smooth curve, and the position of the steps has to be discovered by asking the contract manufacturer directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's discontinuities in that function. And we, we had to talk to our contract manufacturers to find where those were
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: On one such product the difference between one thousand and five thousand units was enormous while the difference between five and ten thousand barely altered the strategy, which is what makes locating the steps worth the effort.
claims.quote_verbatim: One and five. Yeah. One and five is gargantuan.
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: A small producer building fifty or a hundred units instead of a thousand accepts a substantially higher unit price in exchange for a much smaller cash outlay and correspondingly lower risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got to go out and produce 50 or 100, right? You know, just to recoup, you know, my costs and lower my risk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Comical Keyzer Comes a-Callin'

claims.claim_text: The same disadvantage extends beyond parts to logistics, since a small supplier cannot obtain the bulk shipping rates a large operation negotiates.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're a small-time supplier, you don't get the same bulk discounts that a big operation does as far as shipping goes
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Comical Keyzer Comes a-Callin'

claims.claim_text: Designing around an off-the-shelf enclosure imports someone else's volume, which is why it is nearly always cheaper than commissioning a custom one.
claims.quote_verbatim: You get built-in economy of scale, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Magnets, China & IEEE - Xenomorphic Xerox Xebec

claims.claim_text: Vendors will machine and punch a standard enclosure to order, which is not cheap in itself but becomes reasonable at high volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's always cheaper to use an off-the-shelf part than to do something custom.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Magnets, China & IEEE - Xenomorphic Xerox Xebec

claims.claim_text: Standardising an enclosure profile across successive versions of a product spreads the tooling investment over several generations rather than charging it to one, which is what makes injection moulding affordable to a small company.
claims.quote_verbatim: if Bus Pirate version 4, 5, 6, 7 all use that same profile, then our investment in injection mold is, you know, we can drag that out over some time
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Standardising a connector across a product family is likewise a deliberate route to volume, since consolidating on one part is what produces the quantity needed to bring its cost down.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're trying to consolidate, like, Seed Studio are trying to consolidate on this type of connector
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Interconnectorama

claims.claim_text: Ordering an assembled batch large enough to obtain a volume price removes the ability to change the design until the whole batch is sold, which is a direct cost in inflexibility.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't change the design until you've sold all 1,000 of them
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Owning the assembly line resolves that tension by allowing small on-demand batches, so a product can be revised continuously without accumulating obsolete inventory — one company produced around thirty versions of a board in a year, each cheaper or more reliable than the last.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the space of a year, we'll have maybe 30 different versions of a board
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Large manufacturers dominate through scale to the extent that products aimed at narrow audiences are simply not made, because neither the manufacturer nor the retailer wants to operate at that volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of products designed for kind of more niche audiences just don't get made
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: What efficient small-batch manufacturing and internet distribution change is not the existence of mass production but its monopoly, allowing a long tail of products to exist alongside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's the end of the monopoly of the blockbuster
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Component prices available to everyone are set by the volumes of the largest consumer products, which is why an inertial sensor costs a few dollars and a positioning module fifteen.
claims.quote_verbatim: Now you can buy a gyroscope for four bucks. Well, that's because they're using them on cell phones.
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: That relationship can be exploited deliberately by reading the parts list of a high-volume consumer product, on the reasoning that whatever a major manufacturer designs in will be widely available and cheap.
claims.quote_verbatim: if Apple's buying it, there's going to be lots of copies
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: Customer expectations are anchored to products amortised over volumes no small manufacturer can reach, so a device made in ten thousands is compared against a phone and judged expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: here's what it would cost to make an iPhone. You only sell 10,000 of them.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: That anchoring imposes a price ceiling that can push a small producer deliberately toward inexpensive products, since a costly one invites comparison with mass-market hardware it cannot match.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have this price ceiling
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: A niche product escapes the comparison entirely, since buyers accept a premium where nothing else is available and scale is therefore not required to have a viable business.
claims.quote_verbatim: People will pay a premium because they know it's sort of niche.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: Working in a niche is also what allows manufacturing to stay in a high-cost country, because the premium charged covers the absence of volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're working in a niche industry, you know, there's a premium you charge for that sort of thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Alan Yates - Recondite Radiation Raconteur

claims.claim_text: A workable strategy for a first production run is to break even deliberately, building it the expensive way to validate the market and treating the efficiencies not yet taken as the margin available once volume arrives.
claims.quote_verbatim: it makes a lot of sense to basically break even on your first batch, do it the expensive way to validate the market
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Low-volume quotations are erratic enough that the price to the customer has to be set with that variability already built in.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to put that into your price in the first place to make sure that you're making enough money based on those low volume quotes
claims.speaker: Josh Lifton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Josh Lifton

claims.claim_text: Industrial and low-volume products are freed from the pressure to optimise every component, since a slightly more expensive part across five thousand units does not materially affect the business.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can use a slightly more expensive part. You don't have to start a penny pinch.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: The same total revenue can arrive as few expensive units or many cheap ones, and the two demand radically different unit costs, so the volume assumption determines what the product can be.
claims.quote_verbatim: the overall money might be the same, but the per unit cost could be radically different
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: The negotiating leverage that comes with volume extends past components to packaging and distribution, and arrives at the scale of millions of units.
claims.quote_verbatim: You should be able to negotiate better prices on all your parts and all the packaging and distribution channels
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Restricting the options offered is how a manufacturing service reaches scale, with a single surface finish and one set of trace and space rules taking the place of a configurable order.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to get to scale, it's a lot easier if you follow the Model T. philosophy, any color
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Reaching a price point can require changing the process rather than negotiating the price: one stencil supplier had a machine's loading system modified so that material could be bought and cut in a form cheap enough to sell at the intended price.
claims.quote_verbatim: finding a manufacturer that would be willing to modify the loading system
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: A competitive advantage frequently rests on manufacturing efficiency and volume rather than on the design itself, which is what makes publishing the design cost so little.
claims.quote_verbatim: oftentimes the competitive advantage is not the knowledge contained within
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tesla, Checklists and Bullies - Emerging External Eupsychics

claims.claim_text: Cloning a product without technical improvement is defended on the ground that reaching a lower price point and the volume behind it is itself a contribution, and disputed on the ground that it is not sufficient contribution.
claims.quote_verbatim: in terms of making it accessible at a lower price point, that is adding value
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Fabrication plants become cheaper to run the longer they operate, since a facility paid off many times over keeps producing at declining cost, and a supporting cluster of chemical and service suppliers grows around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've paid off that fab 10 times over. So the chips just get cheaper and cheaper.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Setting a headline price first and designing the product and its supply chain to meet it inverts the usual sequence, and works with margins that are sustainable but lower than the industry norm.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have sustainable margins, right? But they're lower than most people.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: That strategy is self-reinforcing: a lower price sells more units, more units buy better component pricing and justify automation, and the higher volume also improves measured defect rates because the same product is built millions of times.
claims.quote_verbatim: It actually helps with the scale, right? Because these things are cheaper. We can make more of them.
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Modularity carries a recurring per-unit cost that scales linearly with production, so a flexibility that is cheap at a hundred units becomes expensive enough at millions to justify hiring engineers purely to design it out.
claims.quote_verbatim: that five bucks a month per whatever you're selling like scales linearly
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Here for a reason

claims.claim_text: Concentrating production for efficiency creates a single point of failure, so that one plant going down removes a large share of available parts at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: we got burned by economies of scale during COVID with the chip shortage
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Consolidation compounds that exposure because the merged company's product lines share the same manufacturing route, whereas separate suppliers with their own plants had genuinely different vulnerabilities and lead times.
claims.quote_verbatim: one problem comes along, and it impacts everything
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Scale within a large company also works through order aggregation, since one product line's requirement is treated as part of a much larger order and priced accordingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: as you get larger and larger companies, you find economies of scale because one order looks like a piece of a giant order
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: Two Dads Puzzlin Things Out

claims.claim_text: Deliberate inefficiency has value as insurance against that concentration, though the argument is difficult to make while the efficient arrangement is working.
claims.quote_verbatim: sometimes you have to have inefficiencies
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Recalling Recalls

claims.claim_text: The most advanced production capacity is not what a functioning economy actually depends on, since the shortage that matters is of the ordinary parts used in vehicles and appliances rather than the newest process nodes.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't necessarily need these bleeding edge plants
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Recalling Recalls

claims.claim_text: Acquisition by a larger company is pursued for buying power, with the expectation that the parent's volume advantage will lower the cost of manufacturing a small company's products.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have the, the economy of scale, uh, advantage
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Vertical integration requires enough demand and money behind it to be worth doing, which is why it is available to very large companies and not to small ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: that vertical integration doesn't happen with small companies
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Concentrating manufacturing capacity on one industry also carries the risk of that capacity sitting idle if the industry contracts, whereas making a component sold into many industries spreads the exposure.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're much more at risk for if your specific industry goes down, then you have all this manufacturing capacity sitting idle
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Buyers with sufficient reserves commit to enormous quantities up front rather than ordering a trial batch, and that commitment is part of what secures the price.
claims.quote_verbatim: They won't go, let's buy a hundred thousand and then see how it goes.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Idiorhythmic IPC Inconcinnity

claims.claim_text: At the extreme, securing supply can mean buying out an entire plant's output, which is a straightforward business decision for a company holding large cash reserves that earn nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: Apple talking about buying out an entire, an entire fab's worth of DRAM
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Documentation Is A Waste Of Time

claims.claim_text: Distributors operate on high turnover and thin margins rather than large mark-ups, with one distributor's published figures showing around five percent profit on a billion dollars of revenue.
claims.quote_verbatim: Our revenues are a billion dollars. Wow. That's great. And profits of like 50 million.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Layout, CAD & Raspberry Pi - Kedogenous Kinetic Knowledge

claims.claim_text: The first question before building any connected consumer device is whether custom hardware is needed at all, since a mass-produced tablet or phone costs less than anything achievable in small or medium quantities and can do most of the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: are you sure this isn't just a sensor connecting over Bluetooth or wifi
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: The price of mass-produced consumer hardware is startling enough to reset expectations: a capable tablet at fifty dollars in one market and a multi-function one under twenty in another.
claims.quote_verbatim: I bought a tablet for like $18
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Establishing what users actually need before optimising can eliminate the requirement entirely: a design being optimised for readings every minute turned out to satisfy its users at four readings a day, a thousandfold reduction in the power budget.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you send readings four times a day, people are thrilled.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: A subscription or aggregation model exists partly to obtain buying power on behalf of individuals who would otherwise buy the same items singly.
claims.quote_verbatim: we get a little bit of economies of scale
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Long

claims.claim_text: A small producer's difficulty with volume pricing is the temptation it creates, since buying ten thousand of a component at a tenth the unit price is attractive precisely when demand is least predictable.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I buy 10,000 of this resistor, it's like a penny
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Legend of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: Demand arriving suddenly through a new distribution channel is hard for a one-person operation to absorb, since a distributor whose sales go well moves from nothing to full rate very quickly.
claims.quote_verbatim: they go from zero to 100% really fast
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Legend of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: A shared-cost service becomes cheaper for everyone as participation rises, which is why increasing the number of users is the stated route to lowering its price rather than reducing the service itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: the more people who do this, the cheaper it will get
claims.episode_title: Building wafer.space with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Scaling production is what allows a module's price to fall, chiefly through the component pricing that volume unlocks.
claims.quote_verbatim: We are scaling up production too. So then we can, you know, really start to get economies of scale.
claims.speaker: Maarten Engelen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Maarten Engelen

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor manufacturing consolidates because leading-edge capacity has become too expensive for any but the largest to fund, with individual plants costing billions.
claims.quote_verbatim: economies of scale at the super low, super low geometry, super high cost
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: A company competing against inevitable low-cost copies stays a generation ahead rather than defending the current product, treating the arrival of cheap equivalents as expected and even beneficial for the wider supply of components.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're always one generation ahead
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Building for high volume at low margin is a coherent strategy distinct from pursuing high margins, sustained by selling in quantity rather than by pricing power.
claims.quote_verbatim: We were in the fund margin business where you sold a lot and made money by selling a lot
claims.speaker: Chuck Peddle
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Chuck Peddle - Charismatic Chipmaking Coryphaeus

claims.claim_text: Small-scale and personal fabrication is a deliberately different objective from mass manufacturing, aimed at making things that do not exist rather than reproducing what a mature industry already supplies cheaply.
claims.quote_verbatim: not necessarily mass manufacturing and economies of scale that work in that way
claims.speaker: Nadya Peek
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Where a technology is new, cost reduction waits on whichever variant reaches sufficient volume first, and several variants may persist because different applications need different characteristics.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just a matter of what takes hold, what gets like the critical mass enough to get the cost down
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Innovation Speculation

claims.claim_text: Tooling cost is what dominates a small hardware project's budget, with mould costs alone capable of consuming most of a substantial crowdfunding raise.
claims.quote_verbatim: The mold costs alone would have eaten up most of their $170,000
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns
